div.head: SUBSECT. 3.
By counsel and persuasion, foulness of the fact, men’s, women’s faults, miseries of marriage, events of lust, &c.
div.p: As there be diverse causes of this burning lust, of heroical love; so there be many good remedies to ease and help; amongst which, good counsel and persuasion, which I should have handled in the first place, are of great moment, and not to be omitted. Many are of opinion, that in this blind headstrong passion, counsel can do no good.

l.hi: Quae enim res in se, neque consilium, neque modum

lg.l: Habet, ullo eam consilio regere non potes.
Which thing hath neither judgement, or an end,
How should advice or counsel it amend?
——— Virg. Ecl. 2.Quis enim modus adsit amori?
[… For what limit could there be to love?]

div.p:
But without question, good counsel and advice must needs be of great force, especially if it shall proceed from a wise, fatherly, reverent, discreet person, a man of authority whom the parties do respect, stand in awe of, or from a judicious friend, of itself alone, it is able to divert and suffice. Gordonius the Physician attributes so much to it, that he would have it by all means used in the first place. Amoveatur ab illa, consilio viri quem timet, ostendendo pericula saeculi, judicium inferni, gaudia Paradisi [Let him be brought away from her by the advice of a man he fears, which makes known the danger of worldliness, the damnation of hell, the delights of paradise]. He would have some discreet men to dissuade them, after the fury of passion is a little spent, or by absence allayed; for it is as intempestive at first, to give counsel, as to comfort parents when their children are in that instant departed; to no purpose to prescribe Narcotics, Cordials, Nectarines, potions, Homer’s Nepenthes, or Helena’s Bowl, &c. Non cessabit pectus tundere [She won’t stop beating her breast], she will lament and howl for a season: let passion have his course a while, and then he may proceed, by foreshowing the miserable events and dangers which will surely happen, the pains of hell, joys of Paradise, and the like, which by their preposterous courses they shall forfeit or incur; and ’tis a fit method, a very good means: for what Lib. de beat. vit. cap. 14.Seneca said of vice, I say of love: sine magistro discitur, vix sine magistro deseritur, ’tis learned of itself, but Longo usu didicimus, longa desuetudine dediscendum est [What we learn through long practice must be unlearned through long disuse], Petrarch. epist. lib. 5. 8.hardly left without a Tutor. ’Tis not amiss therefore to have some such overseer, to expostulate and show them such absurdities, inconveniences, imperfections, discontents, as usually follow; which their blindness, fury, madness, cannot
apply unto themselves, or will not apprehend through weakness: and good for them to disclose themselves, to give ear to friendly admonitions. Tell me sweetheart (saith Tryphaena to a lovesick Charmides in Tom. 4 dial. meret.Lucian), what it is that troubles thee; peradventure I can ease thy mind, and further thee in thy suit; and so without question she might, and so mayst thou, if the Patient be capable of good counsel, and will hear at least what may be said.

If he love at all, she is either an honest woman or a whore. If dishonest, let him read or inculcate to him that 5th of Solomon’s Prov., Ecclus. 26, Ambros. lib. 1 cap. 4 in his book of Abel and Cain, Philo Judaeus de mercede mer., Platina’s dial. in Amores, Espencaeus and those three books of Pet. Haedus de contem. amoribus, Aeneas Silvius’ tart Epistle, which he wrote to his friend Nicholas of Wartburg, which he calls medelam illiciti amoris [a remedy for forbidden love], &c. For what’s an whore, as he saith, but a poller of youth, Sanguinem hominum sorbent [They suck in men’s blood].ruin of men, a destruction, a devourer of patrimonies, a downfall of honour, fodder for the devil, the gate of death, and supplement of hell? Contemplatione Idiotae cap. 34. Discrimen vitae, mors blanda, mel felleum, dulce venenum, pernicies delicata, malum spontaneum, &c. [A risk to life, a seductive death, honey full of gall, a sweet poison, an alluring ruin, a voluntary evil, etc.]Talis amor est laqueus animae, &c. [Such love is a noose for the soul, etc.], a bitter honey, sweet poison, delicate destruction, a voluntary mischief, commixtum coenum, sterquilinium [a pile of filth, a dunghill]. And as Pornodidasc. dial. Ital.Pet. Aretine’s Lucretia, a notable quean, confesseth; gluttony, anger, envy, pride, sacrilege, theft, slaughter, were all born that day that a whore began her profession: for as she follows it, her pride is greater than a rich churl’s, she is more envious than the pox, as malicious as melancholy, as covetous as hell. If from the beginning of the world any were mala, pejor, pessima [bad, worse, worst], bad in the superlative degree, ’tis a whore; how many have I undone, caused to be wounded, slain! O Antonia, thou seest what I am without, but within God knows, a puddle of iniquity, a sink of sin, a pocky quean. Let him now that so dotes, meditate on this; let him see the event and success of others, Samson, Hercules, Holofernes, &c., those infinite mischiefs attend it: if she be another man’s wife he loves, ’tis abominable in the sight of God and men: adultery is expressly forbidden in God’s commandment, a mortal sin, able to endanger his soul: if he be such a one that fears God, or have any religion, he will eschew it, and abhor the loathsomeness of his own fact. If he love an honest maid, ’tis to abuse, or marry her: if to abuse, ’tis fornication, a foul fact (though some make light of it), and almost equal to adultery itself. If to marry, let him seriously consider what he takes in hand, look before he leap, as the proverb is, or settle his affections, and examine first the party and condition of his estate and hers, whether it be a fit match, for fortunes, years, parentage, and such other circumstances, an sit suae Veneris [whether she’s the right love for him]. Whether it be likely to proceed: if not, let him wisely stave himself off at the first, curb in his inordinate passion, and moderate his desire, by thinking of some other subject, divert his cogitations. Or if it be not for his good, as Aeneas forewarned by Mercury in a dream, left Dido’s love, and in all haste got him to Sea,

l.hi: Mnestea, Surgestumque vocat fortemque Cloanthem,

lg.l: Classem aptent taciti jubet ———
[He summons Mnestheus, Sergestus and brave Cloanthus,
He tells them to prepare the fleet in silence …]

div.p: and although she did oppose with vows, tears, prayers, and imprecations,

lg.l: ——— nullis ille movetur

l.hi: Fletibus aut illas voces tractabilis audit;

lg.l: [… he is moved by no
Tears, nor does he listen receptively to those words;]

div.p: let thy Mercury-reason rule thee against all allurements, seeming delights, pleasing inward or outward provocations. Thou mayst do this if thou wilt, pater non deperit filiam, nec frater sororem, a father dotes not on his own daughter, a brother on a sister; and why? Because it is unnatural, unlawful, unfit. If he be sickly, soft, deformed, let him think of his deformities, vices, infirmities: if in debt, let him ruminate how to pay his debts: if he be in any danger, let him seek to avoid it: if he have any lawsuit, or other business, he may do well to let his love matters alone and follow it, labour in his vocation, whatever it is. But if he cannot so ease himself, yet let him wisely premeditate of both their estates; if they be unequal in years, she young and he old, what an unfit match must it needs be, an uneven yoke, how absurd and undecent a thing is it, as Lycinus in Tom. 2 in votis. Calvus cum sis, nasum habeas simum, &c. [When you’re bald, have a snub nose, etc.]Lucian told Timolaus, for an old bald crook-nosed knave, to marry a young wench; how odious a thing it is to see an old Lecher! What should a bald fellow do with a comb, a dumb doter with a pipe, a blind man with a looking-glass, and thou with such a wife? How absurd is it for a young man to marry an old wife for a piece of good. But put case she be equal in years, birth, fortunes, and other qualities correspondent, he doth desire to be coupled in marriage, which is an honourable estate, but for what respects? Her beauty belike, and comeliness of person, that is commonly the main object, she is a most absolute form in his eye at least, cui formam Paphia, & Charites tribuere decorum [to whom Venus has given beauty and the Graces charm]; but do other men affirm as much? Or is it an error in his judgement?

l.hi: Fallunt nos oculi vagique sensus,
Oppressa ratione mentiuntur,

lg.l: [Our eyes mislead us, and our capricious senses
Delude our overwhelmed reason,]

div.p:
our eyes and other senses will commonly deceive us; it may be, to thee thyself upon a more serious examination, or after a little absence, she is not so fair as she seems. Quaedam videntur & non sunt [Some things aren’t what they seem to be]; compare her to another standing by, ’tis a touchstone to try, confer hand to hand,
body to body, face to face, eye to eye, nose to nose, neck to neck, &c., examine every part by itself, then all together, in all postures, several sites, and tell me how thou likest her. It may be not she, that is so fair, but her coats, or put another in her clothes, and she will seem all out as fair; as the Ovid.Poet then prescribes, separate her from her clothes: suppose thou saw her in a base beggar’s weed, or else dressed in some old hirsute attires out of fashion, foul linen, coarse raiment, besmeared with soot, colly, perfumed with Opopanax, Sagapenum, Asafoetida, or some such filthy gums, dirty, about some undecent Action or other; or in such a case as In Catharticis lib. 2.Brasavola the Physician found Malatesta his patient, after a potion of Hellebore, which he had prescribed: Manibus in terram depositis, & ano versus coelum elevato (ac si videretur Socraticus ille Aristophanes, qui Geometricas figuras in terram scribens, tubera colligere videbatur) atram bilem in album parietem injiciebat, adeoque totam cameram, & se deturpabat, ut, &c. [with hands placed on the ground and anus lifted up to the sky (and looking like that follower of Socrates in Aristophanes, who, when drawing geometric diagrams on the ground, seemed to be gathering truffles), he ejected black bile on to the white wall, indeed over the whole room, and defiled himself, so that, etc.], all-to berayed, or worse; if thou sawst her (I say) wouldst thou affect her as thou dost? Suppose thou beheldest her in a Si ferveat deformis ecce formosa est, si frigeat formosa jam sit informis [If an ugly woman is warm, then look: she’s beautiful! If a beautiful woman is cold, she’s hideous]. Th. Morus Epigram.frosty morning, in cold weather, in some passion or perturbation of mind, weeping, chafing, &c., rivelled and ill-favoured to behold. She many times that in a composed look seems so amiable and delicious, tam scitula forma [such a pretty face], if she do but laugh or smile, makes an ugly sparrow-mouthed face, and shows a pair of uneven, loathsome, rotten, foul teeth; she hath a black skin, gouty legs, a deformed crooked carcass under a fine coat. It may be for all her costly tires she is bald, and though she seem so fair by dark, by candlelight, or afar off at such a distance, as Callicratidas observed in Amorum dial. Tom. 4.Lucian, If thou shouldst see her near, or in a morning, she would appear more ugly than a beast; Hugo de claustro Animae, lib. 1 cap. 1.si diligenter consideres, quid per os & nares & caeteros corporis meatus egreditur, vilius sterquilinium nunquam vidisti [if you’d carefully inspect what comes out of the mouth, nostrils and other bodily passages, you’d never see a more disgusting dunghill]. Follow my counsel, see her undressed, see her, if it be possible, out of her attires, furtivis nudatam coloribus [stripped of her stolen colours], it may be she is like Aesop’s Jay, or Hist. nat. 11 cap. 35. A fly that hath golden wings but a poisoned body.Pliny’s Cantharides, she will be loathsome, ridiculous, thou wilt not endure her sight: or suppose thou sawst her sick, pale, in a consumption, on her deathbed, skin and bones, or now dead, cujus erat gratissimus amplexus, as Bernard saith, erit horribilis aspectus [she, whose embrace was the most pleasurable … will be a horrible sight];

lg.l: Non redolet, sed olet, quae redolere solet.
[She who used to be fragrant doesn’t smell good, but reeks.]

div.p: As a posy, she smells sweet, is most fresh and fair one day, but dried up, withered, and stinks another. Beautiful Nireus, by that Homer so much admired, once dead, is more deformed than Thersites, and Solomon deceased as ugly as Marcolphus: thy lovely mistress, that was erst
dearer to thee than thine eyes, once sick or departed, is
worse than any dirt or dunghill. Her embraces were not so acceptable, as now her looks be terrible: thou hadst better behold a Gorgon’s head, than Helena’s carcass.

Some are of opinion, that to see a woman naked is able of itself to alter his affection; and it is worthy of consideration, saith Apol. pro Raym. Seb.Montaigne the Frenchman in his Essays, that the skilfullest masters of amorous dalliance, appoint for a remedy of venerous passions, a full survey of the body; which the Poet insinuates,

l.hi: Ille quod obscaenas in aperto corpore partes

lg.l: Viderat, in cursu qui fuit, haesit amor.
The love stood still, that ran in full career,
When once it saw those parts should not appear.

div.p: It is reported of Seleucus King of Syria, that seeing his wife Stratonice’s bald pate, as she was undressing her by chance, he could never affect her after. Raimundus Lullius the Physician, spying an ulcer or canker in his mistress’ breast, whom he so dearly loved, from that day following abhorred the looks of her. Philip the French King as Nubrigensis lib. 4 cap. 24 relates it, married the King of Denmark’s daughter, and after he had used her as a wife one night, because her breath stunk, they say, or for some other secret fault, sent her back again to her father. Peter Mattheus in the life of Lewis the eleventh, finds fault with our English Hall and Grafton belike.Chronicles, for writing how Margaret the King of Scots’ daughter and wife to Lewis the 11th French King, was ob graveolentiam oris [because of fetid breath] rejected by her husband. Many such matches are made for by-respects, or some seemly comeliness, which after honeymoon’s passed, turn to bitterness: for burning lust is but a flash, a gunpowder passion; and hatred oft follows in the highest degree, dislike and contempt.

lg.l: ——— Juvenal.Cum se cutis arida laxat,
Fiunt obscuri dentes ———
[… When her skin’s dry and flabby,
Her teeth turn dark …]

div.p: when they wax old, and ill-favoured, they may commonly no longer abide them.

lg.l: ——— Jam gravis es nobis,
[… Now you’re repulsive to me,]

div.p: be gone, they grow stale, fulsome, loathsome, odious, thou art a beastly filthy quean,

lg.l: ——— Mart.faciem Phoebe cacantis habes,
[… you’ve got the face, Phoebe, of someone shitting,]

div.p: thou art Saturni podex [Saturn’s anus], withered and dry, insipida & vetula [tasteless and old],

lg.l: ——— Hor. ode 13 lib. 4.Te quia rugae turpant, & capitis nives,
[… because your wrinkles disfigure you, and your head of snowy hair,]

div.p: (I say) be gone, Tully in Cat.portae patent, profiscere [the doors are open: go!].

Yea but you will infer, your mistress is complete, of a most absolute form in all men’s opinions, no exceptions can be taken at her, nothing may be added to her person, nothing detracted, she is the mirror of women for her beauty, comeliness and pleasant grace, unimitable, merae delitiae, meri lepores [pure deliciousness, pure charm], she is myrothecium Veneris, Gratiarum pixis [the ointment box of Venus, the casket of the Graces], a mere magazine of natural perfections, she hath all the Veneres, and Graces,

lg.l: ——— mille faces & mille figuras,
[… a thousand enticements and a thousand features,]

div.p: in each part absolute and complete,

l.hi: Laeta genas, laeta os roseum, vaga lumina laeta:

lg.l: [Lovely cheeks, lovely rosy lips, lovely fluttering eyes:]

div.p: to be admired for her person, a most incomparable, unmatchable piece, aurea proles, ad simulachrum alicuius numinis composita [a golden child, made in the image of some god], a Phoenix, vernantis aetatulae Venerilla [a blooming, tender little Venus], a Nymph, a Fairy, Qualis fuit Venus cum fuit virgo, balsamum spirans, &c. [Such as Venus was when she was a virgin, breathing balsam, etc.]like Venus herself when she was a maid, nulli secunda [second to none], a mere quintessence, flores spirans & amaracum, foeminae prodigium [breathing flowers and marjoram, a marvel of a woman]: put case she be, how long will she continue?

l.hi: Florem decoris singuli carpunt dies:

lg.l: [Each day plucks off a flower of beauty:]

div.p: every day detracts from her person, and this beauty is bonum fragile [a brittle gift], a mere flash, a Venice glass, quickly broken,

l.hi: Anceps forma bonum mortalibus,

lg.l: ——— exigui donum breve temporis,
[Beauty, dubious gift to mortals,
… a trifling and short-lived gift,]

div.p: it will not last. As that fair flower Camerarius emb. 68 cent. 1. Flos omnium pulcherrimus statim languescit, formae typus [This flower, the most beautiful of all, withers instantly: the character of beauty].Adonis, which we call an Anemone, flourisheth but one month, this gracious all-commanding beauty fades in an instant. It is a jewel soon lost, the painter’s Goddess, falsa veritas [a feigned truth], a mere picture. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vanity, Prov. 31. 30.

l.hi: Vitrea gemmula, fluxaque bullula, candida forma est,

lg.l: Nix, Rosa, ros, ventus, fumus & aura, nihil.
A brittle Gem, bubble, is beauty pale,
A Rose, dew, snow, smoke, wind, air, naught at all.

div.p:
If she be fair, as the saying is, she is commonly a fool: if proud, scornful, sequiturque superbia formam [and pride attends beauty], or dishonest, rara est concordia formae atque pudicitiae [rare is the combination of beauty and decency], can she be fair and honest too? Pausanias Lacon. lib. 3.Ariston the son of Agasicles married a Spartan lass, the fairest Lady in all Greece next to Helen, but for her conditions the most abominable, and beastly creature of the world. So that I would wish thee to respect, with Epist. 76.Seneca, not her person but qualities. Will you say that’s a good blade which hath a gilded scabbard, embroidered with gold, and jewels? No, but that which hath a good edge and point, well-tempered metal, able to resist. This beauty is of the body alone, and what is that, but as Orat. 3.Gregory Nazianzen telleth us, a mock of time and sickness? Or as Boethius, as mutable as a flower, and ’tis not nature so makes us, but most part the infirmity of the beholder. For ask another, he sees no such matter: dic mihi per gratias qualis tibi videtur, I pray thee tell me how thou likest my sweetheart, as she asked her sister in Aristaenetus, Epist. 11.whom I so much admire, methinks he is the sweetest gentleman, the properest man that ever I saw: but I am in love, I confess (nec pudet fateri [it’s no shame to admit it]), and cannot therefore well judge. She suspects her judgement, as
well she might, and so mayst thou. But be she fair indeed, golden-haired, as Anacreon his Bathyllus (to examine particulars), she have

l.hi: Flammeolos oculos, collaque lacteola,

lg.l: [Glittering eyes and a milk-white neck,]

div.p: a pure sanguine complexion, little mouth, coral lips, white teeth, soft and plump neck, body, hands, feet, all fair and lovely to behold, composed of all graces, elegances, an absolute piece,

l.hi: Lumina sint Melitae Junonia, dextra Minervae,

lg.l: Mamillae Veneris, sura maris dominae, &c.
[Let the eyes of Melita come from Juno, her hands from Minerva,
Her breasts from Venus, her calf from the goddess of the sea, etc.]

div.p: Let Bebelius adagiis ger.her head be from Prague, paps out of Austria, belly from France, back from Brabant, hands out of England, feet from Rhine, buttocks from Switzerland, let her have the Spanish gait, the Venetian tire, Italian complements and endowments;

l.hi: Candida syderiis ardescant lumina flammis,
Sudent colla rosas, & cedat crinibus aurum,
Mellea purpureum depromant ora ruborem,
Fulgeat, ac Venerem coelesti corpore vincat,

lg.l: Forma dearum omnis, &c.
[Let her shimmering eyes gleam with starry flames,
Let her neck be dewed with roses, and let her hair shine more than gold,
Let her honeyed lips bring forth brilliant red,
Let her glisten, and with her heavenly body surpass Venus,
And all the gods in her beauty, etc.]

div.p:
Let her be such a one throughout, as Lucian deciphers in his Imagines, as Euphranor of old painted Venus, Aristaenetus describes Lais, another Helena, Chariclea, Leucippe, Lucretia, Panthea, Pandora; let her have a box of beauty to repair herself still, such a one as Venus gave Phaon, when he carried her over the Ford; let her use all helps art and nature can yield; be like her, and her, and whom thou wilt, or all these in one; a little sickness, a Fever, smallpox, wound, scar, loss of an eye, or limb, a violent passion, a distemperature of heat or cold, mars all in an instant, disfigures all; childbearing, old age, that tyrant time will turn Venus to Erinnys; raging time, care, rivels her upon a sudden; after she hath been married a small while, and the black ox hath trodden on her toe, she will be so much altered, and wax out of favour, thou wilt not know her. One grows too fat, another too lean, &c., modest Matilda,
pretty pleasing Peg, sweet-singing Susan, mincing merry Moll, dainty dancing Doll, neat Nancy, Jolly Joan, nimble Nell, kissing Kate, bouncing Bess with black eyes, fair Phyllis with fine white hands, fiddling Frank, tall Tib, slender Sib, &c., will quickly lose their grace, grow fulsome, stale, sad, heavy, dull, sour, and all at last out of fashion. Ubi jam vultus argutia, suavis suavitatio, blandus risus, &c. [Where now are the twinkling looks, the sweet charm, the seductive laugh, etc.?] Those fair sparkling eyes will look dull, her soft coral lips will be pale, dry, cold, rough, and blue, her skin rugged, that soft and tender superficies will be hard and harsh, her whole complexion change in a moment, and as M. Drayton.Matilda writ to King John,

l.hi: I am not now as when thou sawst me last,
That favour soon is vanished and past;
That Rosy blush lapt in a Lily vale,

lg.l: Now is with morphew overgrown and pale.

div.p: ’Tis so in the rest, their beauty fades as a tree in winter, which Deianira hath elegantly expressed in the Poet,

l.hi: Deforme solis aspicis truncis nemus?
Sic nostra longum forma percurrens iter,
Deperdit aliquid semper, & fulget minus,
Malisque minus est quidquid in nobis fuit,
Olim petitum cecidit, & partu labat,
Materque multum rapuit ex illa mihi,

lg.l: Aetas citato senior eripuit gradu.
And as a tree that in the greenwood grows,
With fruit and leaves, and in the Summer blows,
In winter like a stock deformed shows:
Our beauty takes his race and journey goes,
And doth decrease, and lose, and come to naught,
Admir’d of old, to this by childbirth brought:
And mother hath bereft me of my grace,
And crooked old age coming on apace.

div.p:
To conclude with Chrysostom, When thou seest a fair and beautiful person, a brave Bona-roba, a bella Donna, quae salivam moveat, lepidam puellam & quam tu facile ames [who makes your mouth water, a pretty girl and one you could easily love], a comely woman, having bright eyes, a merry countenance, a shining lustre in her look, a pleasant grace, wringing thy soul, and increasing thy concupiscence; bethink with thyself that it is but earth thou lovest, a mere excrement, which so vexeth thee, which thou so admirest, and thy raging soul will be at rest. Take her skin from her face, and thou shalt see all loathsomeness under it, that beauty is a superficial skin and bones, nerves, sinews: suppose her sick, now rivelled, hoary-headed, hollow-cheeked, old; within she is full of filthy phlegm, stinking, putrid, excremental stuff: snot and snivel in
her nostrils, spittle in her mouth, water in her eyes, what filth in her brains, &c. Or take her at best, and look narrowly upon her in the light, stand near her, nearer yet, thou shalt perceive almost as much, and love less, as Subtil. 13.Cardan well writes, minus amant qui acute vident [those who see clearly love less], though Scaliger deride him for it: if he see her near, or look exactly at such a posture, whosoever he is, according to the true rules of symmetry and proportion, those I mean of Albertus Durer, Lomatius and Taisnier, examine him of her. If he be elegans formarum spectator [a connoisseur of beauty], he shall find many faults in Physiognomy, an ill colour, ill form, one side of the face likely bigger than the other, or crooked nose, bad eyes, prominent veins, concavities about the eyes, wrinkles, pimples, red streaks, freckens, hairs, warts, neves, inequalities, roughness, scabredity, paleness, yellowness, and as many colours as are in a Turkey-cock’s neck, many indecorums in their parts; est quod desideres, est quod amputes [there’s something you’re missing, there’s something you’d lop off], one leers, another frowns, a third gapes, squints, &c. And ’tis true that he saith, Cardan. subtil. lib. 13.Diligenter consideranti raro facies absoluta, & quae vitio caret, seldom shall you find an absolute face without fault, as I have often observed; nor in the face alone is this defect or disproportion to be found; but in all the other parts, of body and mind; she is fair indeed, but foolish; pretty, comely and decent, of a majestical presence, but peradventure imperious, unhonest, acerba, iniqua [bitter, spiteful], self-willed: she is rich, but deformed; hath a sweet face, but bad carriage, no bringing up, a rude and wanton flirt; a neat body she hath, but is a nasty quean otherwise, a very slut, of a bad kind. As flowers in a garden have colour some, but no smell, others have a fragrant smell, but are unseemly to the eye; one is unsavoury to the taste as rue, as bitter as wormwood, and yet a most medicinal cordial flower, most acceptable to the stomach; so are men and women; one is well qualified, but of ill proportion, poor and base: a good eye she hath, but a bad hand and foot, foeda pedes & foeda manus, a fine leg, bad teeth, a vast body, &c. Examine all parts of body and mind, I advise thee to enquire of all. See her angry, merry, laugh, weep, hot, cold, sick, sullen, dressed, undressed, in all attires, sites, gestures, passions, eat her meals, &c., and in some of these you will surely dislike. Yea not her only let him observe, but her parents how they carry themselves: for what deformities, defects, encumbrances of body or mind be in them at such an age, they will likely be subject to, be molested in like manner, they will patrizare or matrizare [take after father or mother]. And withal let him take notice of her companions, in convictu (as Guevara prescribes), & quibuscum conversetur, whom she converseth with.

lg.l: Noscitur ex Comite, qui non cognoscitur ex se.
[A man not known from himself is known from his company.]

div.p: According to Thucydides, she is commonly the best, de quo minimus foras habetur sermo, that is least talked of abroad. For if she be a noted reveller, a gadder, a singer, a pranker or a dancer, then take heed of her. For what saith Theocritus?

l.hi: At vos festivae ne ne saltate puellae,
En malus hircus adest in vos saltare paratus,

lg.l: [But stop dancing, pretty girls,
Look! An evil he-goat’s here, ready to jump on you,]
Young men will do it when they come to it.

div.p: Fauns and Satyrs will certainly play reaks, when they come in such wanton Bacchos’ or Elenoras’ presence. Now when they shall perceive any such obliquity, indecency, disproportion, deformity, bad conditions, &c., let them still ruminate on that, and as Lib. de contem. amoribus. Earum mendas volvant animo, saepe ante oculos constituant, saepe damnent [Let them turn their defects over in their minds, set them frequently before their eyes and frequently condemn them].Haedus adviseth out of Ovid, earum mendas notent, note their faults, vices, errors, and think of their imperfections; ’tis the next way to divert and mitigate Love’s furious headstrong passions; as a Peacock’s feet, and filthy comb, they say, make him forget his fine feathers, and pride of his tail; she is lovely, fair, well favoured, well qualified, courteous and kind, but if she be not so to me, what care I how kind she be. I say with In delitiis.Philostratus, formosa aliis, mihi superba [beautiful to others, insolent to me], she is a tyrant to me, and so let her go. Besides these outward naeves or open faults, errors, there be many inward infirmities, secret, some private (which I will omit), and some more common to the sex, sullen fits, evil qualities, filthy diseases, in this case fit to be considered; consideratio faeditatis mulierum, menstruae imprimis, quam immundae sunt, quam Savonarola proponit regula septima penitus observanda [Savonarola, in his seventh rule, declares that the consideration of the foulness of women, principally of the menses, and how filthy they are, should be thoroughly attended to]; & Platina dial. amoris fuse perstringit [reflects on this at length], Lodovicus Bonaciolus mulieb. lib. 2 cap. 2, Pet. Haedus, Albertus, & infiniti fere medici [and an almost infinite number of doctors]. A Lover in Calcagninus’ Apologues, wishes with all his heart he were his mistress’ Ring, to hear, embrace, see, and do I know not what: O thou fool, quoth the Ring, if thou werst in my room, thou shouldst hear, observe, and see pudenda & poenitenda [things to be ashamed and repented of], that which would make thee loathe and hate her, yea peradventure all women for her sake.

I will say nothing of the vices of their minds, their pride, envy, inconstancy, weakness, malice, self-will, lightness, insatiable lust, jealousy; Ecclus. 25. 14, No malice to a woman’s, no bitterness like to hers, Eccles. 7. 28, and as the same Author urgeth Prov. 31. 10, Who shall find a virtuous woman? He makes a question of it. Ter. Heaut. act. 4 sc. 1.Neque jus, neque bonum, neque aequum sciunt, melius pejus, prosit, obsit, nihil vident nisi quod libido suggerit. They know neither equity, good nor bad, be it better or worse (as the Comical Poet hath it), beneficial or hurtful, they will do what they list.

l.hi: Insidiae humani generis, querimonia vitae,
Exuviae noctis, durissima cura diei,

lg.l: Poena virum, nex & juvenum, &c. ———
[Snares of mankind, grievances of life,
Ravagings of the night, harshest disquiet of the day,
Torment of grown men, and slaughter of youths, etc ….]

div.p: And to that purpose were they first made, as Jupiter insinuates in the See our English Tatius lib. 1.Poet;

l.hi: The fire that bold Prometheus stole from me,
With plagues call’d women shall revenged be,
On whose alluring and enticing face,

lg.l: Poor mortals doting shall their death embrace.

div.p: In fine, as Diogenes concludes in Nevisanus, Nulla est foemina quae non habeat Quid [there’s no woman that doesn’t have something {you’d complain about}]: they have all their faults.

l.note: Chaucer in Romance of the Rose.
l.hi: Every each of them hath some vice,
If one be full of villainy,
Another hath a liquorish eye.
If one be full of wantonness,
Another is a Chideress.

div.p: When Leander was drowned, the inhabitants of Sestos consecrated Hero’s Lantern to Anteros, Anteroti sacrum, Calcagninus.and he that had good success in his love, should light the candle: but never any man was found to light it; which I can refer to naught, but the inconstancy and lightness of women.

l.hi: For in a thousand, good there is not one;
All be so proud, unthankful and unkind,
With flinty hearts, careless of others’ moan,
In their own lusts carried most headlong blind,
But more herein to speak I am forbidden,

lg.l: Sometime for speaking truth one may be chidden.

div.p:
I am not willing, you see, to prosecute the cause against them, and therefore take heed you mistake me not, Hor.matronam nulla, ego tango [I’m not referring to any married women], I honour the sex, with all good men, and as I ought to do, rather than displease them, I will voluntarily take the oath which Mercurius Britannicus took, Viragin. descript. lib. 2 fol. 95, Me nihil unquam mali nobilissimo sexui, vel verbo, vel facto machinaturum, &c. [that I’ll never plot any mischief against the most noble sex, in either word or deed, etc.], let Semonides,
Mantuan, Platina, Pet. Aretine, and such women-haters bear the blame, if aught be said amiss; I have not writ a tenth of that which might be urged out of them and others; Christoph. Fonseca.non possunt invectivae omnes, & satyrae in foeminas scriptae, uno volumine comprehendi [all the invectives and satires written against women cannot be bound in a single volume]. And that which I have said (to speak truth) no more concerns them than men, though women be more frequently named in this Tract; (to Apologize once for all) I am neither partial against them, or therefore bitter: what is said of the one, mutato nomine [by changing the name], may most part be understood of the other. My words are like Passus’ picture in Encom. Demosthen.Lucian, of whom, when a good fellow had bespoken an horse to be painted with his heels upward, tumbling on his back, he made him passant: now when the fellow came for his piece, he was very angry, and said, it was quite opposite to his mind; but Passus instantly turned the Picture upside down, showed him the horse at that site which he requested, and so gave him satisfaction. If any man take exception at my words, let him alter the name, read him for her, and ’tis all one in effect.

But to my purpose: if women in general be so bad (and men worse than they) what a hazard is it to marry? Where shall a man find a good wife, or a woman a good husband? A woman a man may eschew, but not a wife: wedding is undoing (some say), marrying marring, wooing woeing: a wife is a fever hectic, as Scaliger calls her, and not to be cured but by death, as out of Menander, Dipnosophist. lib. 13 cap. 3.Athenaeus adds,

lg.l: In pelagus te jacis negotiorum, ———

l.hi: Non Libyum, non Aegaeum, ubi ex triginta non pereunt
Tria navigia: ducens uxorem servatur prorsus nemo:

lg.l: Thou wadest into a sea itself of woes;
In Libyc and Aegean each man knows
Of thirty not three ships are cast away,
But on this rock not one escapes, I say.

div.p: The worldly cares, miseries, discontents, that accompany marriage, I pray you learn of them that have experience, for I have none; Synesius.παῖδας ἐγὼ λόγους ἐγεννησάμην, libri mentis liberi [I’ve spawned treatises as children; books are the children of the mind]. For my part I’ll dissemble with him,

l.hi: Este procul nymphae, fallax genus este puellae,

lg.l: Vita jugata meo non facit ingenio: Me juvat, &c.
[Keep well away, brides! Keep away, deceitful tribe of girls!
Married life doesn’t suit my nature: I like, etc.]

div.p: many married men exclaim at the miseries of it, and rail at wives downright; I never tried, but as I hear some of them say,

l.hi: Mare haud mare, vos mare acerrimum,

lg.l: [The sea’s no sea: you’re the cruellest sea,]

div.p: an Irish Sea is not so turbulent and raging as a litigious wife.

l.hi: Scylla & Charybdis Sicula contorquens freta,

lg.l: Minus est timenda, nulla non melior fera est.
Scylla and Charybdis are less dangerous,
There is no beast that is so noxious.

div.p: Which made the Devil belike, as most interpreters hold, when he had taken away Job’s goods, corporis & fortunae bona, health, children, friends, to persecute him the more, leave his wicked wife, as Pineda proves out of Tertullian, Cyprian, Austin, Chrysostom, Prosper, Gaudentius, &c., ut novum calamitatis inde genus viro existeret, to vex and gall him worse quam totus infernus, than all the fiends in hell, as knowing the conditions of a bad woman. Jupiter non tribuit homini pestilentius malum [Jupiter has not bestowed a more pestilent evil to man], saith Semonides: better dwell with a Dragon or a Lion, than keep house with a wicked wife, Ecclus. 25. 16. Better dwell in a wilderness, Prov. 21. 19. No wickedness like to her, Ecclus. 25. 21. She makes a sorry heart, an heavy countenance, a wounded mind, weak hands, and feeble knees, ver. 25. A woman and death are two the bitterest things in the world: uxor mihi ducenda est hodie, id mihi visus est dicere, abi domum & suspende te [‘I must take a wife today’: to me this seemed to be saying, ‘Go home and hang yourself’], Ter. And. 1. 5. And yet for all this we Bachelors desire to be married, with that Vestal virgin, we long for it,

lg.l: Seneca.Felices nuptae! moriar, nisi nubere dulce est.
[Happy brides! Let me die if it’s not sweet to marry.]

div.p: ’Tis the sweetest thing in the world, I would I had a wife, saith he,

lg.l: For fain would I leave a single life,
If I could get me a good wife.

div.p: Heigh-ho for an husband cries she, a bad husband, nay the worst that ever was is better than none: O blissful marriage, O most welcome marriage, and happy are they that are so coupled: we do earnestly seek it, and are never well till we have effected it. But with what fate? Like those birds in the Amator. Emblem. 19.Emblem, that fed about a cage, so long as they could fly away at their pleasure, liked well of it; but when they were taken and might not get loose, though they had the same meat, pined away for sullenness, and would not eat. So we commend marriage,

lg.l: ——— donec miselli liberi,

l.hi: Aspicimus dominam; sed postquam heu janua clausa est,
Fel intus est quod mel fuit:

lg.l: [… while we’re wretched free men,
We admire our mistress; but alas, once the door is closed,
What was honey inside is now gall:]

div.p: so long as we are wooers, may kiss and coll at our pleasure, nothing is so sweet, we are in heaven as we think: but when we are once tied, and have lost our liberty, marriage is an hell, give me my yellow hose again: a mouse in a trap lives as merrily, we are in a purgatory some of us, if not hell itself. Dulce bellum inexpertis [War is sweet to those who haven’t experienced it], as the proverb is, ’tis fine talking of war, and marriage sweet in contemplation, till it be tried: and then as wars are most dangerous, irksome, every minute at death’s door, so is, &c. When those wild Irish Peers, saith De rebus Hibernicis lib. 3.Stanihurst, were feasted by King Henry the second (at what time he kept his Christmas at Dublin) and had tasted of his Princelike cheer, generous wines, dainty fare, had seen his massy plate of silver, gold, enamelled, beset with jewels, golden candlesticks, goodly rich hangings, brave furniture, heard his trumpets sound, Fifes, Drums, and his exquisite music in all kinds: when they had observed his majestical presence as he sat in purple robes, crowned with his sceptre, &c., in his royal seat, the poor men were so amazed, enamoured, and taken with the object, that they were pertaesi domestici & pristini tyrotarichi [sick of the plain native diet they had before], as weary and ashamed of their own sordidity and manner of life. They would all be English forthwith; who but English! But when they had now submitted themselves, and lost their former liberty, they began to rebel some of them, others repent of what they had done, when it was too late. ’Tis so with us Bachelors, when we see and behold those sweet faces, those gaudy shows that women make, observe their pleasant gestures and graces, give ear to their Siren tunes, see them dance, &c., we think their conditions are as fine as their faces, we are taken with dumb signs, in amplexum ruimus [we rush into the embrace], we rave, we burn, and would fain be married. But when we feel the miseries, cares, woes, that accompany it, we make our moan many of us, cry out at length and cannot be released. If this be true now, as some out of experience will inform us, farewell wiving for my part, and as the Comical Poet merrily saith,

l.note: Eubulus in Crisil. Athenaeus dipnosophist. lib. 13 cap. 3.
l.hi: Perdatur ille pessime qui foeminam
Duxit secundus, nam nihil primo imprecor!

lg.l: Ignarus ut puto mali primus fuit.
Translated by my brother Ralph Burton.Foul fall him that brought the second match to pass,
The first I wish no harm, poor man alas,
He knew not what he did, nor what it was.

div.p: What shall I say to him that marries again and again,

l.hi: Stulta maritali qui porrigit ora capistro,

lg.l: [Who puts his silly head into the matrimonial bridle,]

div.p: I pity him not, for the first time he must do as he may, bear it out sometimes by the head and shoulders, and let his next neighbour ride, or else run away, or as that Gomesius de sale lib. 3 cap. 7.Syracusian in a tempest, when all ponderous things were to be exonerated out of the ship, quia maximum pondus erat [because she was the biggest burden], fling his wife into the Sea. But this I confess is Comically spoken, Haec in speciem dicta cave ut credas [Beware of believing these words, spoken in pretence].and so I pray you take it. In sober sadness, Bachelors always are the bravest men. Bacon. Seek eternity in memory, not in posterity, like Epaminondas, that instead of children, left two great victories behind him, which he called his two daughters.marriage is a bondage, a thraldom, an yoke, an hindrance to all good enterprises (he hath married a wife and cannot come), Qui cupit uxorem litem cupit atque dolorem [He who desires a wife desires strife and sorrow].a stop to all preferments, a rock on which many are saved, many impinge and are cast away: not that the thing is evil in itself or troublesome, but full of all contentment and happiness, one of the three things which please God, Ecclus. 25. 1.when a man and his wife agree together, an honourable and happy estate, who knows it not? If they be sober, wise, honest, as the Poet infers,

l.hi: Si commodos nanciscantur amores,

lg.l: Nullum iis abest voluptatis genus.
If fitly match’d be man and wife,
No pleasure’s wanting to their life.

div.p: But to undiscreet sensual persons, that as brutes are wholly led by sense, it is a feral plague, many times an hell itself, and can give little or no content, being that they are often so irregular and prodigious in their lusts, so diverse in their affections. Uxor nomen dignitatis, non voluptatis, as Aelius Verus imperator [Emperor Aelius Verus]. Spar. vit. ejus.he said, a wife is a name of honour, not of pleasure: she is fit to bear the office, govern a family, to bring up children, sit at board’s end and carve, as some carnal men think and say; they had rather go to the stews, or have now and then a snatch as they can come by it, borrow of their neighbours, than have wives of their own; except they may, as some Princes and great men do, keep as many Courtesans as they will themselves, fly out impune [with impunity],

l.hi: Permolere uxores alienas,

lg.l: [Screw other men’s wives,]

div.p:
or that polygamy of Turks, Lex Julia, which Caesar once enforced in Rome (though Levinus Torrentius, and others suspect it) uti uxores quot & quas vellent liceret, that every great man might marry, and keep as many wives as he would, or Irish divorcement were in use: but as it is, ’tis hard and gives not that
satisfaction to these carnal men, beastly men as too many are: Quod licet ingratum est [What’s permitted is displeasing].what still the same? To be tied For better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, &c., ’tis durus sermo [a hard speech] to a sensual man.to one, be she never so fair, never so virtuous, is a thing they may not endure, to love one long. Say thy pleasure, and counterfeit as thou wilt, as Ter. act. 1 Sc. 2 Eunuch.Parmeno told Thais, neque tu uno eris contenta, one man will never please thee; nor one woman many men: but as Lucian. Tom. 4.Pan replied to his father Mercury, when he asked whether he was married, Nequaquam pater, amator enim sum, &c., No father, no, I am a lover still, and cannot be contented with one woman. Pythias, Echo, Maenades, and I know not how many besides were his Mistresses, he might not abide marriage. Varietas delectat [Variety delights], ’tis loathsome and tedious, what one still? Which the Satirist said of Iberina, is verified in most,

l.hi: Unus Iberinae vir sufficit? ocyus illud
Extorquebis ut haec oculo contenta sit uno,

lg.l: ’Tis not one man will serve her by her will,
As soon she’ll have one eye as one man still:

div.p: as capable of any impression as materia prima [primordial matter] itself, that still desires new forms, like the sea their affections ebb and flow. Husband is a cloak for some to hide their villainy; once married she may fly out at her pleasure, the name of Husband is a sanctuary to make all good. Eo ventum (saith Seneca) ut nulla virum habeat, nisi ut irritet adulterum [We’ve come to the point … where no woman will have a husband, except to provoke her lover]. They are right and straight, as true Trojans as mine host’s daughter, that Spanish wench in Lib. 28.Ariosto, as good wives as Messalina. Many men are as constant in their choice, and as good husbands as Nero himself, they must have their pleasure of all they see, and are in a word far more fickle than any woman.

l.hi: For either they be full of jealousy,
Or masterful, or love novelty, &c.

div.p: Good men have often ill wives, as bad as Xanthippe was to Socrates, Elenora to St. Lewis, Isabella to our Edward the second: and good wives are as often matched to ill husbands, as Mariamne to Herod, Serena to Diocletian, Theodora to Theophilus, and Thyra to Gurmunde. But I will say nothing of dissolute and bad husbands, of Bachelors and their vices; their good qualities are a fitter subject for a just volume, too well known already in every village, town and city, they need no blazon; and lest I should mar any matches, or dishearten loving maids, for this present I will let them pass.

Being that men and women are so irreligious, depraved by nature, so wandering in their affections, so brutish, so subject to disagreement, so unobservant of marriage rites, what shall I say? If thou beest such a one, or thou light on
such a wife, what concord can there be, what hope of agreement? ’Tis not conjugium [joining together] but conjurgium [quarrelling together], as the Reed and Fern in the Camerar. 82 cent. 3.Emblem, averse and opposite in nature: ’tis twenty to one thou wilt not marry to thy contentment: but as in a lottery forty blanks were drawn commonly for one prize, out of a multitude you shall hardly choose a good one: a small ease hence then, little comfort,

lg.l: Semonides.Nec integrum unquam transiges laetus diem.
[Nor shall you ever spend a whole day happy.]
If he or she be such a one,
Thou hadst much better be alone.

div.p: If she be barren, she is not ——— &c. If she have Children make misfortunes more bitter, Bacon.children, and thy state be not good, though thou be wary and circumspect, thy charge will undo thee,

lg.l: ——— faecunda domum tibi prole gravabit,
[… a fertile woman will burden your home with offspring,]

div.p:
thou wilt not be able to bring them up, Heinsius Epist. Primerio.and what greater misery can there be, than to beget children, to whom thou canst leave no other inheritance but hunger and thirst? Chrys. Fonseca.Cum fames dominatur, strident voces rogantium panem, penetrantes patris cor [When hunger reigns, their shrieking cries beg for bread, piercing their father’s heart]: what so grievous as to turn them up to the wide world, to shift for themselves? No plague like to want: and when thou hast good means, and art very careful of their education, they will not be ruled. Think but of that old proverb, ἡρώων τέκνα πήματα Heroum filii noxae [the children of heroes are calamities], great men’s sons seldom do well; O utinam aut coelebs mansissem, aut prole carerem! [oh, if only I’d stayed single, or not had children!] Liberi sibi carcinomata [To him children were cancers].Augustus exclaims in Suetonius. Jacob had his Reuben, Simeon and Levi: David an Amnon, an Absalom, Adonijah; wise men’s sons are commonly fools, insomuch that Spartian concludes, Neminem prope magnorum virorum optimum & utilem reliquisse filium [almost no great man has left a good and useful son]; they had been much better to have been childless. ’Tis too common in the middle sort; thy son’s a drunkard, a gamester, a spendthrift; thy daughter a fool, a whore, thy servants lazy drones and thieves, thy neighbours devils, they will make thee weary of thy life. Lemnius cap. 6 lib. 1.If thy wife be froward, when she may not have her will, thou hadst better be buried alive; she will be so impatient, raving still, and roaring like Juno in the Tragedy, there’s nothing but tempests, all is in an uproar. If she be soft and foolish, thou werst better have a block, she will shame thee and reveal thy secrets: if wise and learned, well qualified, there is as much danger on the other side, mulierem doctam ducere
periculosissimum [it’s most perilous to marry a learned woman], saith Lib. 2 numer. 101 sil. nup.Nevisanus, she will be too insolent and peevish,

lg.l: Juvenal.Malo Venusinam quam te Cornelia mater.
[I’d prefer a girl from Venusia to you, mother Cornelia.]

div.p: Take heed; if she be a slut, thou wilt loathe her; if proud she’ll beggar thee, Tom. 4 Amores.she’ll spend thy patrimony in baubles, all Arabia will not serve to perfume her hair, saith Lucian: if fair and wanton, she’ll make thee a Cornuto; if deformed, she will paint. Idem.If her face be filthy by nature, she will mend it by art, alienis & adscititiis imposturis [by strange, imported tricks], which who can endure? If she do not paint she will look so filthy, thou canst not love her, and that peradventure will make thee unhonest. Cromerus lib. 12 hist. relates of Casimirus, that he was unchaste, because his wife Adelaide the daughter of Henry Landgrave of Hassia, was so deformed. If she be poor, she brings beggary with her (saith Nevisanus), misery and discontent. If you marry a maid, it is uncertain how she proves,

l.hi: Haec forsan veniet non satis apta tibi:

lg.l: [This one might become unsuitable for you:]

div.p: if young, she is likely wanton and untaught; if lusty, too lascivious; and if she be not satisfied, you know where and when, nil nisi jurgia [nothing but quarrelling], all is in an uproar, and there is little quietness to be had: if an old maid, ’tis an hazard she dies in childbed: if a rich Sil nup. lib. 2 num. 55. Dives inducit tempestatem, pauper curam: ducens viduam se inducit in laqueum [A rich woman brings a storm, a poor one, anxiety; in marrying a widow you put your neck in a noose].widow, induces te in laqueum, thou dost halter thyself, she will make all away beforehand, to her other children, &c.

lg.l: ——— dominam quis possit ferre tonantem?
[… Who can put up with a domineering mistress?]

div.p: She will hit thee still in the teeth with her first husband: if a young widow, she is often unsatiable and immodest. If she be rich, well descended, bring a great dowry, or be nobly allied, thy wife’s friends will eat thee out of house and home, Sic quisque dicit alteram ducit tamen [So everyone says, yet still they marry another one].dives ruinam aedibus inducit [a rich woman brings the house to ruin], she will be so proud, so high-minded, so imperious. For

lg.l: ——— nihil est magis intolerabile dite,
[… nothing’s more unbearable than a rich woman,]

div.p:
there’s nothing so intolerable, thou shalt be as the Tercel of a goshawk, Petrarch.she will ride upon thee, domineer as she list, wear the breeches in her oligarchical government, and beggar thee besides. Uxores divites servitutem exigunt
[Rich wives require slavery], as Seneca hits them (declam. lib. 2 declam. 6), dotem accepi, imperium perdidi [I took the dowry, I lost the power]. They will have sovereignty, pro conjuge dominam arcessis [you bring in a governess for a wife], they will have attendance, they will do what they list. If a woman nourish her husband, she is angry and impudent, and full of reproach, Ecclus. 25. 24. Scilicet uxori nubere nolo meae [Of course I don’t want my wife to be my husband].In taking a dowry thou losest thy liberty, dos intrat, libertas exit, hazardest thine estate.

l.hi: Hae sunt atque aliae multae in magnis dotibus

lg.l: Incommoditates, sumptusque intolerabiles, &c.
[These and many other disadvantages
And intolerable expenses come with big dowries, etc.]

div.p: with many such inconveniences: say the best, she is a commanding servant; thou hadst better have taken a good housewife maid in her smock. Since then there is such hazard, if thou be wise, keep thyself as thou art, ’tis good to match, much better to be free.

lg.l: ——— Plautus mil. glor. act. 3 sc. 1.procreare liberos lepidissimum,
Hercle vero liberum esse, id multo est lepidius.
[… It’s most delightful to produce children,
But, my god, it’s much more delightful to be free!]

div.p: Stobaeus ser. 66. Alex. ab Alexand. lib. 4 cap. 8.Art thou young? Then match not yet; if old, match not at all.

l.hi: Vis juvenis nubere? nondum venit tempus,

lg.l: Ingravescente aetate jam tempus praeteriit.
[You want to marry young? The time’s not yet come.
As the years get more painful, the time’s already passed.]

div.p: And therefore with that Philosopher, still make answer to thy friends that importune thee to marry, adhuc intempestivum, ’tis yet unseasonable, and ever will be.

Consider withal how free, how happy, how secure, how heavenly, in respect, a single man is, Ter.as he said in the Comedy, Et isti quod fortunatum esse autumant, uxorem nunquam habui, and that which all my neighbours admire and applaud me for, account so great an happiness, I never had a wife; consider how contentedly, quietly, neatly, plentifully, sweetly and how merrily he lives! He hath no man to care for but himself, none to please, no charge, none to control him, is tied to no residence, no cure to serve, may go and come, when, whither, live where he will, his own master, and do what he list himself. Consider the excellency of Virgins, They shall attend the lamb in heaven because they were not defiled with women, Apoc. 14.Virgo coelum meruit [the virgin is worthy of heaven], Hieron.marriage replenisheth the earth, but virginity Paradise; Elias, Eliseus, John Baptist were
Bachelors: Virginity is a precious Jewel, a fair garland, a never-fading flower; for why was Daphne turned into a green bay-tree, but to show that virginity is immortal?

l.hi: Ut flos in septis secretus nascitur hortis,
Ignotus pecori, nullo contusus aratro,

lg.l: Quam mulcent aurae, firmat Sol, educat imber, &c.

l.hi: Sic virgo dum intacta manet, dum chara suis, sed

lg.l: Cum Castum amisit, &c. ———
[As the hidden flower grows in the walled garden,
Unknown to the beasts, torn up by no plough,
Which the breezes soothe, the sun strengthens, the rain nourishes, etc.
Such is the virgin while she stays untouched, while she’s precious to her own, but
When she’s lost her chastity, etc ….]

div.p: Virginity is a fine picture, as Diet. salut. cap. 22. Pulcherrimum sertum infiniti precii, gemma, et pictura speciosa [A most beautiful garland of infinite worth, a gem and a splendid picture].Bonaventure calls it, a blessed thing in itself, and if you will believe a Papist, meritorious. And although there be some inconveniences, irksomeness, solitariness, &c., incident to such persons, want of those comforts, quae aegro assideat & curet aegrotum, fomentum paret, roget medicum, &c. [someone to attend and look after you when you’re sick, prepare the poultice, call for the doctor, etc.], embracing, dalliance, kissing, colling, &c., those furious motives and wanton pleasures a new-married wife most part enjoys; yet they are but toys in respect, easily to be endured, if conferred to those frequent encumbrances of marriage; solitariness may be otherwise avoided with mirth, music, good company, business, employment; in a word, Mart.Gaudebit minus, & minus dolebit [he’ll have less joy and less pain]; for their good nights, he shall have good days. And methinks sometime or other amongst so many rich Bachelors, a benefactor should be found to build a monastical College for old, decayed, deformed, or discontented maids to live together in, that have lost their first loves, or otherwise miscarried, or else are willing howsoever to lead a single life. The rest I say are toys in respect, and sufficiently recompensed by those innumerable contents and incomparable privileges of Virginity. Think of these things, confer both lives, and consider last of all these commodious prerogatives a Bachelor hath, how well he is esteemed, how heartily welcome to all his friends, quam mentitis obsequiis, as Tertullian observes, with what counterfeit courtesies they will adore him, follow him, present him with gifts, hamatis donis [baited gifts]: it cannot be believed (saith Lib. 24.Ammianus), with what humble service he shall be worshipped, how loved and respected: if he want children (and have means) he shall be often invited, attended on by Princes, and have advocates to plead his cause for nothing, as Lib. de amore prolis.Plutarch adds. Wilt thou then be reverenced, and had in estimation?

lg.l: ——— dominus tamen & domini rex

l.hi: Si tu vis fieri, nullus tibi parvulus aula
Luserit Aeneas, nec filia dulcior illa?

lg.l: Jucundum & charum sterilis facit uxor amicum.
[… But if you want to be a lord, and a lord’s master,
There should be no little Aeneas playing in your hall,
Nor an even sweeter daughter there.
A barren wife makes you a dear and pleasing friend.]

div.p: Live a single man, marry not, and thou shalt soon perceive how those Haeredipetae [legacy hunters] (for so they were called of old) will seek after thee, bribe and flatter thee for thy favour, to be thine heir or executor: Arruntius and Haterius, those famous parasites in this kind, as Annal. 11.Tacitus and 6to de benefic. cap. 38.Seneca have recorded, shall not go beyond them. Periplectomenes that good personate old man, delitium senis [a delight of an old man], well understood this in Plautus; for when Pleusicles exhorted him to marry that he might have children of his own, he readily replied in this sort,

l.hi: Quando habeo multos cognatos, quid opus mihi sit liberis?

lg.l: Nunc bene vivo & fortunate, atque animo ut lubet.
Mea bona mea morte cognatis dicam interpartiant.

l.hi: Illi apud me edunt, me curant, visunt quid agam, ecquid velim,

lg.l: Qui mihi mittunt munera, ad prandium ad coenam vocant.
Whilst I have kin, what needs I brats to have?
Now I live well, and as I will, most brave.
And when I die, my goods I’ll give away,
To them that do invite me every day,
That visit me, and send me pretty toys,
And strive who shall do me most courtesies.

div.p: This respect thou shalt have in like manner, living as he did, a single man. But if thou marry once, E Graeco.cogitatio in omni vita te servum fore, bethink thyself what a slavery it is, what an heavy burden thou shalt undertake, how hard a task thou art tied to (for as Jerome hath it, qui uxorem habet, debitor est, & uxoris servus alligatus [he who has a wife is a debtor, and a slave shackled to her]), and how continuate, what squalor attends it, what irksomeness, what charges; for wife and children are a perpetual bill of charges; besides a Myriad of cares, miseries, and troubles; for as that Comical Plautus merrily and truly said, he that wants trouble, must get to be master of a ship, or marry a wife; and as another seconds him, wife and children have undone me; so many, and such infinite encumbrances accompany this kind of life. Furthermore, uxor intumuit [the wife became angry], &c., or as he said in the Comedy,

lg.l: Ter. Adelph.Duxi uxorem, quam ibi miseriam vidi, nati filii, alia cura.
[I took a wife, and what misery I’ve seen! Sons were born: more worry!]

div.p: All gifts and invitations cease, no friend will esteem thee, and thou shalt be compelled to lament thy misery, and make thy moan with Itineraria in psalmos instructione ad lectorem.Bartholomaeus Scheraeus, that famous Poet Laureate, and professor of Hebrew in Wittenberg: I had finished this work long since, but that inter alia dura & tristia quae misero mihi pene tergum fregerunt (I use his own words), amongst many miseries which almost broke my back, συζυγία ob Xantipismum [being yoked to Xanthippism], a shrew to my wife, tormented my mind above measure, and beyond the rest. So shalt thou be compelled to complain, and to cry out at last, with Bruson. lib. 7, 22 cap.Phoroneus the lawyer, How happy had I been, if I had wanted a wife! If this which I have said will not suffice, see more in Lemnius lib. 4 cap. 13 de occult. nat. mir., Espencaeus de continentia, lib. 6 cap. 8, Kornmann de virginitate, Platina in Amor. dial., Practica artis amandi, Barbarus de re uxoria, Arnisaeus in polit. cap. 3, and him that is instar omnium [worth all of them], Nevisanus the Lawyer, Sylva nuptial., almost in every page.
